Other than the stuttered rise and fall of his chest, he was completely out. “Kind of surprised he even made it this far.” Jake sat back against another seat, using his shoulder to keep Leon from sliding off to one side. “No kidding.” Meg watched him for a moment, trying to not focus too hard on the way random muscles seemed to shiver in him. “...if he’s down... now what?” “Fuck,” Jake muttered, scrubbing a hand through his hair. “Okay. Okay, think.” They still had a gen left. The prime triad. Worst possible spot. No cover. No soft choke points. Herman would patrol it hard — like he always did — just waiting for someone dumb enough to risk a touch. If Claudette could solo it, maybe they could run interference. Pull Herman wide and get him chasing. It’s not like he and Meg weren’t fast enough to volley him back and forth. But then what? Even if the last gen popped... Even if the gates opened... Even if Herman didn’t catch them before they reached it... How in the hell were they supposed to carry him? Assuming they could get him semi-alert and mobile again, his shoulder was shot. His legs were unreliable at best. There was no way in hell he was going to make it across the yard, through a gate, into the Fog, and out the other side in this state. And even if they dragged him through... Jake glanced over. The bruises. The scorch marks . This wasn’t a trial injury. It was environmental. Would the Fog even heal it? Passing through the Fog via the gates or hatch had a significantly lower impact on the body than anything else, usually only glossing over whatever they had failed to repair en-route. Survivors had been returning to camp for weeks now with random injuries that were barely scabbed over, provided they didn’t get them from a killer or a hook. He looked at Meg. She looked back. Neither said a word. Leon wheezed softly between them — breath like it was playing tug-of-war with gravity. And they both knew. This wasn’t going to work. They needed another way out. Chapter 6: Bargaining Chip The waiting room was dim, sterile, and still. Just beyond the cracked glass of the entrance, the Fog crept like a living thing, curling and slinking along the floor. The quiet was thick. Unnatural. Claudette found them not long after finishing the generator she'd been working on. There was only one left to go, but she knew she couldn’t head back toward that hallway — not after the screams that had followed her out. Instead, she'd traced the outer ring of rooms, hunting for Meg. She spotted them in a waiting room four hallways over. A quick scan around the area told her Herman hadn’t found them yet. No static buzz. No shadowed figure rounding the corner. Nothing. Ducking quickly inside, her eyes locked on Leon. Relief hit first — he was free. The cuffs were gone. But then the rest of the picture registered, and relief twisted into alarm. He was slumped back against the chairs, barely upright, his legs sprawled on the floor like someone had just dropped him there and walked away. Jake was braced on one side, body curved in to keep Leon from tipping, his full focus on the angry red marks scorched across Leon’s wrist. Every few seconds, Leon’s chest hitched in a shallow, rasping breath. Nothing else moved. Claudette shed her jacket without a word and bunched it behind Leon’s head, trying to cushion the harsh angle where seat met neck. The moment she leaned him back against it, he sighed — small and breathy, but real. It settled something sharp in her chest. "Is he going to be ok, do you think?" Meg looked up from across the room. "He's alive, somehow." Meg was pacing in a tight loop nearby, boots scuffing against the tiled floor, arms crossed so tight it looked like she might snap her own ribs. Every few seconds, she flicked a glance toward the corridor like she expected the Doctor to appear out of nowhere. Claudette dropped to her knees beside the boys, careful and methodical despite the obvious panic in her face. She placed two fingers at Leon’s neck, then moved his chin gently to check for responsiveness. There was a hitch in his breathing, a rattling catch that made her shoulders tense. His eyes were unfocused, pupils blown entirely too wide. If he recognized her at all, it didn’t show. He didn’t seem to be unconscious — more suspended between asleep and catatonic — but at least he didn’t seem to be actively crashing in that exact moment. Small favor from the Fog, she supposed. If they could survive multiple cuts, toxins, and being impaled on hooks with nothing more than a band-aid, maybe something in the Fog was keeping him going too. It was more than she’d expected, honestly. This kind of thing wasn’t her wheelhouse. She could handle bleeding, treat infections, even splint a limb if she had to. But this? This was something else entirely. Still, she was the closest thing they had to a medic. That had to count for something. Right? Her hands trembled as she pulled back, brushing a fleck of ash from his collarbone. “He’s stable. Kind of.” Claudette breathed. “But only just. There’s... not much I can do without real tools. Or meds. Or time. I don’t know if the Fog's going to patch this fully on its own." Meg shook her head. "We can try to carry him to the gate, at least. Hope the transition does enough to stabilize him." Claudette hesitated. “The Fog heals trial injuries. We know that. Bleeding, bruises, broken bones... if it happened as part of the trial, it gets fixed. Mostly. But... this?” She gestured softly to Leon. “This wasn’t one wound. It’s systemic. Burnout.
